sections.body: A database row or a log line can be updated in place, and nothing about its neighbors changes. A hash pointer removes that silence. Block n stores H(block n-1), where H is SHA-256, a function for which no one knows how to find two different inputs with the same output. Change one byte of an old block and its hash changes, so the pointer stored in the next block no longer matches. This is tamper evidence, not tamper prevention: the bytes can still be edited, but a verifier notices. The rest of this unit adds the other pieces in order: Merkle trees commit to many transactions at once, signatures say who authorized them, proof of work makes extending the chain expensive, and fork choice decides which extension counts.

sections.body: The program defines a block as a height, the previous block's hash and a payload. encode turns a block into bytes with a fixed field order, big-endian fixed-width integers and a length prefix in front of the variable payload; hash is sha256.Sum256 over exactly those bytes. firstBrokenLink checks every block against its predecessor and returns the first height where either the height sequence or the hash pointer fails. The run records the tip, edits an old payload, and then plays an attacker who rewrites every later pointer.
sections.title: Build and verify a chain with crypto/sha256
sections.walkthrough: build starts from the all-zero hash for genesis and feeds each block's hash into the next block. After the payload at height 1 changes, height 2 is the first block whose Prev no longer equals hash(chain[1]), so the verifier reports 2 rather than a bare false. Rewriting Prev at heights 2 and 3 makes every link consistent again, so the chain on its own looks valid; only the comparison with the tip recorded before the edit exposes it. The printed values are the first four bytes of each 32-byte digest.

sections.body: The hash covers bytes, not meaning. Two nodes that agree a block says alice pays bob 5 but serialize it differently compute different hashes and then disagree about the whole chain. encode avoids that by construction, and its length prefix also removes ambiguity at field boundaries: without it, a payload "ab" followed by a field "c" and a payload "a" followed by "bc" would hash identical bytes. Text formats are where this usually goes wrong. JSON objects are unordered, whitespace is insignificant, a number has several spellings (5, 5.0, 5e0), and Go's encoding/json adds its own choices: it sorts map keys, writes struct fields in declaration order and escapes <, > and & unless told otherwise.
sections.title: Pick one byte encoding and never let it drift
sections.walkthrough: The three literal strings decode to the same object yet print three different digests, 8cd4d93c, 560a0696 and 39350022, so a verifier that re-serializes before hashing accepts or rejects data depending on which form it happens to produce. json.Marshal sorts the map keys and writes the memo as a\u003cb; an Encoder with SetEscapeHTML(false) writes a<b and appends a newline, trimmed here. Both outputs are valid JSON, and neither is a hashing format unless one canonicalization scheme, such as RFC 8785, is applied everywhere.

sections.body: The relinking step in the first program is the realistic attack. Whoever can rewrite one block can usually recompute every later hash in microseconds. What the chain buys you is that one 32-byte value, the tip hash, commits to the entire history, so protecting history reduces to protecting that value. Publish it, sign it, store it in a system with different administrators, or make producing a replacement expensive, which is what proof of work and proof of stake do later in this unit. Audit logs, release manifests and blockchains share this structure and differ in who is trusted to produce or hold the tip. When verification fails, report the first broken height and treat every later block as unverified until it is checked against a trusted tip again; an operator needs to know which record and which neighbor disagree.
sections.title: Anchor the tip, or the chain proves nothing

sections.body: Check in known-answer vectors: a fixed block and its expected digest, so a refactor that reorders fields or changes an integer width fails a test instead of silently forking your history. Mutate each field in turn and assert that the hash changes. Fuzz pairs of blocks with go test -fuzz and assert that different blocks never encode to the same bytes, which catches a missing length prefix. Keep a single encode function shared by writer and verifier; two implementations of one format is how nodes come to disagree. Test the verifier on an empty chain, a lone genesis block, a height gap and an edited genesis. SHA-256 appears here because it is in the standard library; Ethereum uses Keccak-256, a different function, as the signing-boundaries lesson explains.
sections.title: Test the encoding like a consensus rule

readings.takeaway: Hash one canonical byte encoding of each block, verify every link from genesis, report the first break, and keep the trusted tip hash out of reach of anyone who can edit the data.

designGuide.cost: About 2n hashes to build the tree and log2(n) per proof, plus a tree shape that becomes a frozen consensus rule once roots are published.
strengths: A proof costs about log2(n) hashes, not the whole block.

readings.hint: Think about what a 64-byte leaf made of two sibling hashes would hash to.
readings.introduction: A block header cannot carry every transaction, but it can carry one 32-byte Merkle root that commits to all of them. A client that trusts the header can then check that a particular transaction is included from a handful of sibling hashes instead of the whole block. The tree shape and hashing rules are consensus rules, and two classic mistakes let different transaction lists produce the same root.
readings.nuance: Without prefixes, H(left || right) is also the leaf hash of the 64-byte string left || right, so a shorter forged list reaches the same root. Prefixes make leaf and node inputs disjoint; the odd-leaf rule is a separate fix.
readings.objective: Build a domain-separated Merkle tree, generate and verify inclusion proofs, and explain the duplicate-leaf and second-preimage pitfalls.
readings.question: A Merkle tree hashes leaves as H(data) and interior nodes as H(left || right). Which attack do distinct leaf and node prefixes stop?
readings.reviewAnswer: So no interior node can pose as a leaf

sections.body: The previous lesson chained blocks. Inside a block the problem is different: thousands of transactions, and a wallet or indexer that wants to check one of them without downloading the rest. A Merkle tree hashes each transaction into a leaf, then hashes pairs of nodes level by level until one root remains, and the header stores only that root. To prove leaf i, the prover sends the sibling at each level on the path from the leaf to the root, and the verifier recomputes the path and compares. For n leaves that is about log2(n) hashes, so 20 hashes cover a million transactions. A proof shows that the leaf is committed by this root; it says nothing about whether the header itself is canonical, which is the job of the chain and fork-choice lessons.
sections.title: One root for many transactions

sections.body: The program hashes leaves with a 0x00 prefix and interior nodes with a 0x01 prefix, and promotes a lone last node to the next level unchanged instead of pairing it with a copy of itself. prove collects one sibling per level when one exists; verify walks up from the leaf and uses the claimed index and the tree size to decide, at every level, whether the sibling sits left or right. The second half builds the classic tree, with no prefixes and duplication of the last hash, to show what the two rules prevent.
sections.title: Build, prove and verify in Go
sections.walkthrough: With five leaves, leaf 2 needs three siblings: leaf 3, the hash of leaves 0 and 1, and leaf 4, which was promoted from below. A changed leaf or a claimed index of 3 recomputes a different path and fails. verify derives each direction from index and size instead of trusting flags inside the proof, and it rejects proofs with too few or too many hashes. naiveRoot gives [a b c] and [a b c c] one root and accepts two 64-byte forged leaves built from interior hashes; the separated tree rejects both. Promotion yields the same tree shape as RFC 6962, which splits at the largest power of two below n.

sections.body: Bitcoin's tree pairs an odd last hash with a copy of itself, so the transaction lists [a, b, c] and [a, b, c, c] produce the same root, exactly as naiveRoot shows. This became CVE-2012-2459. The list with the repeated transaction is an invalid block, but its header hash equals the honest block's. A node that received the mutated version first, rejected it and remembered the header hash as invalid would then refuse the honest block too. Bitcoin Core now detects the mutation while computing the root and treats the block as malformed rather than marking the header invalid, and the comment above its Merkle code warns new designs not to copy the algorithm. In your own trees, promote the lone node or use the RFC 6962 split, and include the leaf count in whatever you sign or publish next to the root.
sections.title: The duplicate-last-leaf trap

sections.body: Without domain separation an interior node is SHA-256 of 64 bytes and a leaf is SHA-256 of arbitrary bytes. Anyone who knows two sibling hashes can present their 64-byte concatenation as a leaf, and the shorter, forged list reaches the same root: that is the second-preimage result in the program. Prefixing leaves with 0x00 and nodes with 0x01, as Certificate Transparency does in RFC 6962, makes the two kinds of input disjoint, so no interior node can satisfy a leaf proof. Bitcoin's tree has no such separation, and its known ambiguity around 64-byte transactions follows from that. Ethereum headers use Merkle-Patricia tries for transactions, receipts and state rather than this binary tree, and eth_getProof (EIP-1186) returns account and storage proofs. The principle is the same: verify the proof against a root you already trust, never against a root delivered in the same response.
sections.title: Separate leaves from interior nodes

sections.body: Take the root from a header you have already validated. Bind the index and tree size into verification so a proof for one position cannot be replayed for another. Reject proofs that are too long or too short instead of ignoring extra hashes. Hash leaves from their canonical bytes, as in the hash-chain lesson. Test every index for many sizes, including 1 and powers of two plus and minus one; a wrong index; swapped sibling order; truncated and extended proofs; and a leaf whose bytes equal an interior node. Fuzz verify with random proofs and require that it never panics. These tests are cheap: checking every index and every wrong index for all sizes from 1 to 40 runs in well under a second.
sections.title: Review checklist for proof code

readings.takeaway: Prefix leaves and interior nodes differently, never duplicate an odd node, and verify a proof from the leaf, its index and the tree size against a root you already trust.
readings.title: Merkle proofs: show one transaction is in a block with about log2(n) hashes

designGuide.cost: One Keccak-256 and one public-key recovery per verification, plus explicit normalization of v at every boundary that accepts signatures.
strengths: The signer is computed, so no public key travels with the data.
Deterministic RFC 6979 nonces make signing reproducible in tests.

readings.hint: Recovery succeeds for both; look for the function that compares s with half the curve order.
readings.introduction: A hash chain shows that data changed; a signature shows who approved it. Ethereum and Bitcoin use ECDSA over the secp256k1 curve, and Ethereum appends a recovery byte so that a verifier can compute the signer's public key from the signature instead of receiving it. Recovery always produces some key, so the code that matters is the comparison with the address you expected and the checks that reject malleable signatures.
readings.nuance: Both signatures recover the same key, so the address comparison passes. ValidateSignatureValues(v, r, s, true) applies EIP-2's s <= N/2 rule, the same check go-ethereum's transaction signers run before recovery.
readings.objective: Sign a Keccak-256 digest with go-ethereum's crypto package, recover and check the signer's address, and enforce the low-s rule on untrusted signatures.
readings.question: crypto.SigToPub recovers the same signer from a signature (r, s) and its twin (r, N-s). Which check rejects the twin before you trust it?
readings.reviewAnswer: ValidateSignatureValues with homestead true

sections.body: crypto.Sign returns 65 bytes: r and s, 32 bytes each, followed by a recovery id v of 0 or 1. r and s form an ordinary ECDSA signature; v tells the recovery algorithm which candidate curve point the signer used, so crypto.SigToPub and crypto.Ecrecover return exactly one public key. That is why an Ethereum transaction carries no public key and no from field: the sender is computed from the signature. The byte encoding of v varies by context. Legacy transactions store 27 or 28, EIP-155 transactions store chainID*2+35 or +36, typed transactions store a yParity of 0 or 1, and personal_sign signatures usually end in 27 or 28. Normalize to 0 or 1 at the boundary before calling the crypto package, and leave transaction encodings to the signers in core/types.
sections.title: What a recoverable signature contains

sections.body: The program derives a test key from 32 bytes of 0x01, a well-known throwaway value that must never hold funds, and it never contacts a network. It signs a Keccak-256 digest, recovers the public key, then edits the message and recovers again. Finally it builds the mirror-image signature (r, N-s) with the recovery bit flipped, where N is the curve order, and runs it through the checks go-ethereum offers.
sections.code:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"math/big"

	"github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/crypto"
)

func main() {
	// TEST KEY ONLY: fixed bytes, never funded, never used on a real network.
	key, err := crypto.ToECDSA(bytes.Repeat([]byte{1}, 32))
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	signer := crypto.PubkeyToAddress(key.PublicKey)
	fmt.Println("test signer:", signer.Hex())

	if _, err := crypto.Sign([]byte("not a digest"), key); err != nil {
		fmt.Println("raw message:", err)
	}

	digest := crypto.Keccak256([]byte("chain 1337: pay bob 5, nonce 7"))
	sig, err := crypto.Sign(digest, key)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	again, _ := crypto.Sign(digest, key)
	fmt.Println("signature:", len(sig), "bytes, v =", sig[64], "deterministic:", bytes.Equal(sig, again))

	pub, err := crypto.SigToPub(digest, sig)
	fmt.Println("recovered == signer:", err == nil && crypto.PubkeyToAddress(*pub) == signer)

	edited := crypto.Keccak256([]byte("chain 1337: pay bob 500, nonce 7"))
	other, err := crypto.SigToPub(edited, sig)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println("edited message: no error, recovered == signer:", crypto.PubkeyToAddress(*other) == signer)

	// Build the high-s twin (r, N-s) with the recovery bit flipped.
	n := crypto.S256().Params().N
	r := new(big.Int).SetBytes(sig[:32])
	s := new(big.Int).SetBytes(sig[32:64])
	twinS := new(big.Int).Sub(n, s)
	twin := make([]byte, 65)
	copy(twin, sig[:32])
	twinS.FillBytes(twin[32:64])
	twin[64] = sig[64] ^ 1

	twinPub, err := crypto.SigToPub(digest, twin)
	fmt.Println("twin recovers signer:", err == nil && crypto.PubkeyToAddress(*twinPub) == signer)
	pubBytes := crypto.FromECDSAPub(&key.PublicKey)
	fmt.Println("low-s rule accepts original:", crypto.ValidateSignatureValues(sig[64], r, s, true),
		"twin:", crypto.ValidateSignatureValues(twin[64], r, twinS, true))
	fmt.Println("VerifySignature original:", crypto.VerifySignature(pubBytes, digest, sig[:64]),
		"twin:", crypto.VerifySignature(pubBytes, digest, twin[:64]))
}
sections.title: Sign and recover with a fixed test key
sections.walkthrough: crypto.Sign refuses the 12-byte string because it requires exactly 32 bytes, so callers must hash first. Signing the same digest twice yields identical bytes because the nonce is derived from the key and the digest as in RFC 6979, with no random source. SigToPub on the edited digest returns no error and a valid but different public key; only the address comparison catches it. The twin recovers the same signer, so recovery alone does not make signatures unique. ValidateSignatureValues with homestead set to true and VerifySignature both reject the twin because its s is above N/2.

sections.body: ECDSA signs a number smaller than the curve order, so it needs fixed-size input; Ethereum uses Keccak-256 and Bitcoin uses double SHA-256. Size is the smaller reason. The go-ethereum documentation for Sign warns that the hash must not be chosen by an adversary. A service that signs whatever 32 bytes a caller supplies is a signing oracle, and those bytes may be the hash of a transaction that spends the service's funds. Hash your own structured message with a prefix that says what it is: accounts.TextHash implements the EIP-191 prefix "\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n" plus the message length, and EIP-712 hashes typed data under a domain. The signing-boundaries lesson covers key custody and domain policy; the rule at the primitive level is that the signer owns the hashing step.
sections.title: Why you sign a digest, never raw input

sections.body: For every valid ECDSA signature (r, s), the pair (r, N-s) is also valid for the same key and message. If any part of a system identifies data by the hash of its signed bytes, a third party can flip s and produce a second valid encoding with a different identifier, without the key. Bitcoin suffered this as transaction-ID malleability, and Ethereum's Homestead upgrade (EIP-2) made transactions with s above N/2 invalid. In go-ethereum the rule is crypto.ValidateSignatureValues(v, r, s, homestead), which the transaction signers call before recovering, and VerifySignature also rejects high s. Ecrecover and SigToPub do not, and EIP-2 deliberately left the on-chain ecrecover precompile accepting high s, so contracts must check it too. When you accept signatures from users, for logins or off-chain orders, validate the values yourself and never key a record by signature bytes.
sections.title: Malleability and the low-s rule

sections.body: Keep the test key fixed and labeled, and assert known answers: the 0x01-repeated key has the address 0x1a642f0E3c3aF545E7AcBD38b07251B3990914F1, so a regression in key derivation fails at once. Write negative tests for a wrong digest, a wrong expected address, the high-s twin, v outside 0 and 1, r or s equal to zero or N, a 64-byte signature without v and a digest of the wrong length. If you ship builds with and without cgo, run the suite both ways: go-ethereum uses the decred secp256k1 package when cgo is off and libsecp256k1 when it is on, and your checks should not depend on which one recovered the key. Prefer fixed vectors to crypto.GenerateKey in tests so that every failure is reproducible.
sections.title: Test the verifier, not just the signer

readings.takeaway: Sign only digests you computed, recover the key and compare its address with the one you expected, and reject high-s or malformed values with ValidateSignatureValues before trusting a signature.

readings.hint: Where does EIP-55 keep its check bits?
readings.introduction: An Ethereum address is neither a public key nor a name. It is the last 20 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of an uncompressed public key, written as 40 hex digits. Those digits carry no error detection unless their letter case follows EIP-55, so a validator has to decide what it accepts before value moves: the format, the checksum, and whether the zero address can ever be a destination.
readings.nuance: EIP-55 hides the checksum in letter case. An all-lowercase string has no case information, so it is valid unchecked hex, and a changed digit simply names a different 20-byte account.
readings.objective: Derive an address from a public key, produce and check EIP-55 checksums, and validate user-supplied addresses, including the zero address.
readings.question: Why can an EIP-55 validator not catch a mistyped digit in an all-lowercase address?
readings.reviewAnswer: None; a typo just names another valid address

sections.body: The signatures lesson recovered a public key: an uncompressed secp256k1 point serialized as 0x04 followed by the 32-byte X and Y coordinates. Ethereum drops the 0x04 prefix, hashes the 64 coordinate bytes with Keccak-256 and keeps the last 20 bytes. crypto.PubkeyToAddress does exactly that, and so does go-ethereum's transaction sender recovery. The mapping is one-way, so an address never yields a key, and not every address belongs to a key at all: a contract's address comes from its creator's address and nonce (CREATE) or from a salt and the init code hash (CREATE2), and nothing in the 20 bytes says which kind you are looking at. Ask the chain for the code at that address when the difference matters.
sections.title: From public key to address

sections.body: The program derives the test key's address by hand and compares it with PubkeyToAddress, re-implements the EIP-55 rule and compares it with common.Address.Hex, then feeds six inputs through parseAddress. That validator requires the 0x prefix and exactly 40 hex digits, enforces the checksum when the input mixes cases, and rejects the zero address. The last three lines show library behavior that regularly surprises reviewers.
sections.title: Derive, checksum and validate in one program
sections.walkthrough: eip55 hashes the 40 lowercase ASCII hex characters, not the 20 raw bytes, and uppercases a letter when its nibble in that hash is 8 or more; digits never change. The flipped input differs from the signer only in the case of one letter and is rejected. The lowercase typo is accepted and names a different account, because lowercase input carries no checksum. MixedcaseAddress.ValidChecksum compares the input with Hex(), so it reports false for any all-lowercase input. A JSON body without a to field, and HexToAddress given non-hex text, both produce the zero address with no error.

sections.body: EIP-55 stores its checksum in letter case: each of the letters a to f is uppercase exactly when the matching nibble of the hash is 8 or more. An address carries about 15 check bits on average, and the EIP estimates that a mistyped checksummed address passes by accident about 0.0247% of the time. An all-lowercase or all-uppercase string has no case information, so EIP-55 treats it as unchecked, and most wallets accept it. Your service has to choose: accept lowercase from machines that produced it, such as an RPC response or your own database, but for destinations a person typed or pasted, require the checksummed form or add a confirmation step. Always display addresses with Hex() so that whatever people copy is checksummed. A few networks use EIP-1191, which mixes the chain ID into the checksum, so a valid case pattern there can fail plain EIP-55.
sections.title: What EIP-55 protects and what it cannot

sections.body: common.HexToAddress never fails. It strips an optional prefix, decodes what hex it can, and pads or crops to 20 bytes, so 0x1234 becomes an address ending in 1234 and garbage becomes the zero address; the abi-calls lesson already warned that it converts rather than validates. common.IsHexAddress checks length and digits but accepts input without a prefix or with 0X and ignores case. Address.UnmarshalJSON requires the prefix and 40 digits but not the checksum, and a missing field leaves the zero value. Put one parser like parseAddress at every boundary: HTTP handlers, CLI flags and configuration. Give the zero address an explicit policy, too. ERC-20 tokens emit it as the sender of a mint and conventionally as the recipient of a burn, and many token contracts reject transfers to it, so as a payout destination it almost always means a missing value rather than an intent.
sections.title: Parsing is not validation

sections.body: Use the mixed-case vectors published in EIP-55, such as 0x5aAeb6053F3E94C9b9A09f33669435E7Ef1BeAed, as known answers for both Hex() and your parser. Add cases for a missing prefix, an uppercase 0X prefix, 39 and 41 digits, non-hex characters, surrounding whitespace, an all-uppercase body, the zero address, and a lowercase address with one digit changed, which passes format checks and must then be caught by an allow-list or a confirmation step downstream. Store addresses as 20 raw bytes or as the canonical Hex() string, never in whatever case the user typed, so that equality checks and unique indexes do not depend on letter case.
sections.title: Test the validator at its edges

readings.takeaway: Derive addresses with PubkeyToAddress, display them with Hex(), and validate input with one explicit parser that checks prefix, length, the checksum on mixed case and the zero address.

readings.hint: Look at what UTXOSet.Apply does to each input once validation passes.
readings.introduction: Every ledger must answer one question before it accepts a payment: has this value already been spent? Bitcoin answers with a set of unspent transaction outputs that each transaction consumes and creates. Ethereum answers with a balance and a nonce per account that each transaction updates. Neither stores a wallet's balance as a primary fact; both derive it from accepted history, and that choice shapes every indexer built on top.
readings.nuance: The first spend deleted genesis:0 and created new outputs. A UTXO ledger keeps no per-account nonce or stored balance; the second spend names a coin that no longer exists.
readings.objective: Implement minimal UTXO and account ledgers in Go, reject double spends in each, and explain what each model makes easy or hard for an indexer.
readings.question: In the UTXO ledger, why is a second transaction that spends genesis:0 rejected?
readings.reviewAnswer: The spent output is deleted from the set
readings.reviewPrompt: How does UTXO stop a double spend?

sections.body: In the UTXO model the state is a set of coins: outputs of earlier transactions, each with an amount and a locking condition. Bitcoin locks outputs with scripts; this lesson uses an owner name. A transaction names the exact outputs it consumes, which disappear, and creates new outputs, usually including change back to the sender, and whatever the inputs hold beyond the outputs is the fee. In the account model the state maps each address to an account with a balance, a nonce and, for contracts, code and storage. A transaction says from, to, value and nonce, and the ledger debits one balance and credits another. The double-spend defense follows from the shape: a UTXO ledger deletes the coin, so a second spend names something that no longer exists; an account ledger demands the next nonce, so a replay is stale.
sections.title: Two shapes of state

sections.body: UTXOSet.Apply checks every input before it changes anything: each must exist, belong to the signer and appear only once, and the outputs may not exceed the inputs. Ledger.Apply checks the nonce and the balance, then debits, credits and increments the nonce. Owner fields stand in for the signature checks that the signatures lesson covers. After the transfers, the program rebuilds the account state from the history of accepted transfers and compares it with the live state.
sections.title: Both ledgers in one program
sections.walkthrough: Alice spends the 50-unit genesis output into 30 for bob and 19 change, and the missing 1 is the fee. Spending genesis:0 again fails because the first Apply deleted it. A transaction listing t1:1 twice would count those 19 units twice; the seen map rejects it before any sum is used. The account ledger rejects the replayed nonce 0 and then a correctly numbered transfer that exceeds the 20 remaining. UTXO balances are computed on demand by summing unspent outputs, and the account state rebuilt from history matches.

sections.body: The seen map in UTXOSet.Apply looks redundant until you remove it. Without it, one transaction can reference the same output twice, the input sum counts the coin twice, and the ledger creates money. This is not hypothetical: CVE-2018-17144 was a Bitcoin Core bug in which an optimization skipped the duplicate-input check during block validation. Nodes running 0.14 could be crashed by such a block, and versions 0.15.0 to 0.16.2 would have accepted one that inflated the supply. Validate everything first and mutate only after every check passes, as both Apply functions do, so that a rejected transaction leaves no partial state. Production code also range-checks every amount (Bitcoin caps values at 21 million coins) and guards unsigned addition against overflow; this model uses small numbers and leaves that out.
sections.title: The duplicate-input check is not optional

sections.body: UTXO makes provenance easy: every payment names its inputs, so tracing where a coin came from is a direct walk, and undoing a block is mechanical, re-adding the outputs it spent and deleting the ones it created, which is what Bitcoin Core's per-block undo data stores. Per-address balance and history are the hard part. An indexer must maintain an owner index over outputs and their spends, and one wallet uses many addresses and change outputs, so a user's balance is an aggregation the chain knows nothing about. The account model makes balances easy, a single read at a chosen block, and hides history: value moves inside contract execution without a top-level transaction, token balances live in contract storage and surface only through logs such as the ERC-20 Transfer event, and full history needs logs or traces. Undoing a block needs the previous value of every key it touched, which the fork-choice lesson uses.
sections.title: What each model means for an indexer

sections.body: The rebuild at the end of the program is the most valuable test either model can have: start from genesis, replay accepted history and compare with the live state. Run it in CI against fixtures and periodically against production projections. Add property tests: total supply stays constant apart from issuance and fees in the UTXO model, or explicit mints and burns in the account model; a rejected transaction changes nothing; applying an accepted transaction a second time is rejected. If a projection keeps a balance column, treat it as a cache of a derivation and keep the means to recompute it, because the chain will never tell you the column drifted.
sections.title: Balances are derived; test that they stay derivable

readings.takeaway: Validate every input or nonce before mutating state, treat balances as derived from accepted history, and choose indexing structures that match how the model records spends.

Typed decode errors do not match ErrCanonInt with errors.Is.
designGuide.cost: Reflection-based encoding is slower than generated code, and a format without field names makes every schema change a versioning decision.
strengths: One canonical byte form per value keeps hashes and signatures stable.
The decoder rejects non-canonical sizes, integers and trailing data.

readings.hint: Think about what happens to a transaction hash when two byte strings mean the same value.
readings.introduction: Ethereum hashes and signs bytes, so every value needs exactly one byte form. On the execution layer that form is Recursive Length Prefix (RLP): transactions, headers and receipts are RLP, and typed transactions are a type byte followed by an RLP payload. RLP encodes byte strings and nested lists and nothing else. go-ethereum's decoder is deliberately strict, because accepting a second spelling of a value means accepting a second hash for it.
readings.nuance: 0x05 and 0x820005 would decode to the same integer but hash differently. Accepting both gives one transaction two identities, and nodes that disagree about acceptance split consensus.
readings.objective: Encode and decode Go structs with go-ethereum's rlp package, recognize the canonical-form rules, and bound untrusted input before decoding it.
readings.question: A lax decoder reads the bytes 0x820005 as the integer 5. Why must a consensus decoder reject them?
readings.reviewAnswer: One value must have exactly one encoding

sections.body: A single byte below 0x80 is its own encoding. A string of 0 to 55 bytes is 0x80 plus its length followed by the bytes; a longer string is 0xb7 plus the length of the length, the length in big-endian, then the bytes. Lists follow the same pattern from 0xc0 and 0xf7. Integers are not a separate type: they are big-endian strings with no leading zero bytes, so zero is the empty string 0x80. go-ethereum maps Go types onto this. Structs become lists of their exported fields in declaration order, unsigned integers and *big.Int become minimal strings, byte slices and arrays become strings, other slices become lists. Signed integers, floats and maps are refused because they have no canonical form, and a negative big.Int returns an error. The hash-chain lesson made these choices by hand; RLP is the standardized version.
sections.title: Two kinds of item and a length prefix

sections.body: The program prints the specification's own examples, round-trips a struct holding an address, a *big.Int and an empty byte slice, then decodes five malformed inputs into a uint64 and one oversized value from a reader with an explicit limit. No network or chain is involved; these are pure functions over bytes.
sections.title: Encode, decode and feed the decoder bad input
sections.walkthrough: 0 encodes as 80, 15 as the single byte 0f and 1024 as 82 04 00; dog is 83 followed by its ASCII bytes, and [cat dog] is the list header c8 over two strings. The 27-byte transfer starts with da (0xc0 + 26), then 07 for the nonce and 94 for the 20-byte address. Each malformed input breaks a different rule: 8105 wraps a byte that must stand alone, 820005 has a leading zero, b80105 uses the long form for a short string, 0f0f leaves trailing bytes, and bbffffffff claims a 4 GiB string inside 5 bytes. io.MultiReader hides the underlying bytes.Reader, as a network connection would, so only the explicit 64-byte limit stops the 100-byte value, and it does so before allocating.

sections.body: Each rejected input is something a lax decoder could interpret: 8105 and 820005 as the integer 5, b80105 as the one-byte string 05. If a node accepted them, one transaction would have several byte forms and therefore several hashes. A node that accepted a form and a node that rejected it would disagree about a block's validity, which is a consensus split. The property that protects everyone is a bijection: decoding b succeeds only if encoding the result gives back b. go-ethereum's Stream enforces it with ErrCanonSize for a size that should have used a shorter form, ErrCanonInt for leading zeros and, in DecodeBytes, ErrMoreThanOneValue for trailing data. Struct decoding also rejects too few or too many list elements unless trailing fields carry the optional or tail tags.
sections.title: Why consensus decoders refuse non-canonical bytes

sections.body: An RLP header can claim a length up to 2^64-1, and a naive decoder allocates what the header says. DecodeBytes, and NewStream over a bytes.Reader, bytes.Buffer or strings.Reader, know the input length and return ErrValueTooLarge for larger claims. Over any other io.Reader, such as a connection or an HTTP body, the stream has no limit unless you pass one, and rlp.Decode offers no way to pass one, as its documentation warns. Cap the raw message first (go-ethereum's eth protocol caps messages at 10 MiB, and its legacy transaction pool refuses transactions over 128 KiB), then decode with NewStream(r, limit). After decoding, bound the values: RLP puts no size limit on *big.Int, so check BitLen, as the transaction pool does for fee caps over 256 bits. One API surprise: when DecodeBytes fills a typed value, canonical-form failures come back wrapped in a descriptive error that errors.Is does not match against ErrCanonInt or ErrCanonSize, so treat any decode error as invalid input.
sections.title: Bound untrusted input before you decode it

sections.body: Check in the specification examples and the RLP fixtures from the ethereum/tests repository as known answers. For every type you decode from outside, fuzz with go test -fuzz: when DecodeBytes succeeds, re-encode and require identical bytes; when it fails, require no panic and no large allocation. Add cases for each rule above, for a nested list whose inner length exceeds its parent (ErrElemTooLarge), for structs with missing or extra elements, and for optional trailing fields. For hot paths, go-ethereum's rlpgen generates reflection-free encoders. Keep RLP where it belongs: it is the execution layer's consensus encoding, the consensus layer uses SSZ, and your own service APIs are better served by formats with field names and explicit schemas.
sections.title: Test with vectors and round trips

readings.takeaway: Let the rlp package define the bytes, cap untrusted input and decode with an explicit stream limit, bound decoded big integers, and treat every non-canonical form as invalid.
readings.title: RLP: Ethereum's canonical encoding, and why its decoder rejects every other spelling
wrongAnswers: RLP stores integers as fixed 8-byte words
Leading zeros are legal but slower to parse

cautions: Security is probabilistic and assumes an honest hash-rate majority.
Timestamps are miner-supplied and need explicit bounds.
designGuide.cost: Real proof of work spends energy and hardware in proportion to the security it buys; the toy costs milliseconds only because its difficulty is tiny.
strengths: Verification cost is constant regardless of difficulty.
Cumulative work gives an objective rule for comparing chains.

readings.hint: The winning nonce is inside the header; what does Valid do with it?
readings.introduction: A hash chain reveals that history changed, but anyone can rebuild a chain. Proof of work makes rebuilding expensive: a block counts only if its header hashes below a target, and the only known way to find such a header is to try nonces. Bitcoin still works this way; Ethereum left proof of work at the Merge in 2022. The idea to keep is the asymmetry between expensive search and cheap verification.
readings.nuance: The verifier does not search. It hashes the header, including the found nonce, once and compares the integer with the target. That asymmetry is what makes proof of work usable.
readings.objective: Mine a toy block against a big.Int target, verify it with one hash, compute its expected work and retarget from observed block times.
readings.question: A miner needed about 2^16 attempts to find a valid nonce. How much work does a node spend verifying that header's proof of work?
readings.reviewAnswer: One header hash compared with the target
readings.reviewPrompt: PoW: cost to verify a block?

sections.body: Read a SHA-256 digest as a 256-bit unsigned integer. A header is valid when that number is below a target, and lowering the target makes valid headers rarer. With a target of 2^(256-k), a valid hash starts with k zero bits, so a miner expects about 2^k attempts while a verifier hashes once and compares. The nonce is the field the miner is free to change. Everything else in the header is fixed: the parent hash, the height, the difficulty and a commitment to the body, such as the Merkle root from the second lesson. Finding a nonce therefore proves work spent on this exact header. Change the body and the commitment changes, the old nonce stops working, and the cheap relinking attack from the first lesson now costs a fresh search for every block rewritten.
sections.title: A target turns hashing into a lottery

sections.body: Header.Hash encodes fixed-width fields in a fixed order, as in the hash-chain lesson, and Valid compares the digest with target(Bits) using math/big. Mine increments the nonce from zero, so the run is deterministic: the same header always yields the same nonce. Work reports the expected number of hashes a target represents, and Retarget scales the target by observed over expected time, clamped to a factor of four. Difficulty stays at 16 bits or less so the run takes milliseconds.
sections.title: Mine, verify and retarget a toy chain
sections.walkthrough: At 8, 12 and 16 bits the expected work is 255, 4095 and 65535 hashes, computed as 2^256 divided by target+1, the formula Bitcoin Core uses for chain work. The 16-bit search took 205064 attempts, about three times the mean; attempt counts are geometrically distributed, so single blocks vary widely. Verification is one Valid call, and flipping one bit of the body commitment makes the same nonce fail. Retarget keeps the target when ten blocks take the expected 6000 seconds, halves it when they take half as long, and clamps a 60-fold speed-up to a factor of four. The spans are fixed numbers, not clock readings.

sections.body: Hash rate rises and falls as hardware joins or leaves, so a fixed target would let block intervals drift from seconds to days. Bitcoin recomputes its target every 2016 blocks from the time those blocks took, aiming at ten minutes per block, and limits each adjustment to a factor of four in either direction; Retarget is that rule in miniature. Timestamps are written by miners, so real rules also bound them: Bitcoin rejects a header whose time is not later than the median of the previous eleven blocks or lies more than two hours in the future. A toy that reads the wall clock is neither deterministic nor representative. Treat timestamps as untrusted data, as the program does, and test the rules that bound them.
sections.title: Difficulty adjustment keeps block time, not security, constant

sections.body: Because work is costly to produce, nodes follow the valid chain with the most cumulative work, and rewriting a block buried under k later blocks means outpacing the rest of the network for k blocks. That security is probabilistic: an attacker with a minority of hash rate can still win a short race, and one with a majority can rewrite at will. Bitcoin's real header is 80 bytes hashed with double SHA-256, its target is packed into a 4-byte bits field, and it accepts a hash equal to the target, where this toy uses a strict comparison so that Bits reads as leading zero bits. Ethereum's proof-of-work era ended with the Merge (EIP-3675); validators now propose blocks and stake finalizes them, which the next lesson relies on. And do not reinvent proof of work as an API rate limiter: puzzles cost honest low-end devices more than attackers with GPUs.
sections.title: What proof of work does and does not secure

sections.body: Keep difficulty tiny in tests and pin the expected nonce for a fixed header as a known answer, so a changed encoding changes the nonce and fails loudly. Test Valid at the boundary: under a strict comparison a hash equal to the target must fail, and a target of zero or above 2^256 must be refused before use; real chains also enforce a maximum target, the proof-of-work limit. Test Retarget at, above and below both clamps, and check integer division, whose rounding compounds over many periods. Benchmark mining separately from unit tests, and never let a test search at a difficulty whose runtime depends on luck you have not measured: the 16-bit search here already needed three times its average.
sections.title: Testing work-based code

readings.takeaway: Proof of work is asymmetric: a nonce below a 2^(256-k) target takes about 2^k hashes to find and one hash to check, so chains compare cumulative work and retarget from timestamps treated as data.
readings.title: Proof of work: finding a nonce takes thousands of hashes, checking it takes one
wrongAnswers: About 2^16 hashes, repeating the search
About 2^8 hashes, the square root of the search

cautions: Confirmations are a probability; recompute them from the head.
latest and safe can both move backwards; only finalized is final.
designGuide.cost: Undo journals for every block, an atomic undo-apply-checkpoint transaction, and roughly 13 minutes of waiting for finality on Ethereum.
strengths: Cumulative work makes every honest node converge on one head.
Per-block undo data turns a reorg into a mechanical replay.

readings.hint: Only one tag is backed by an economic penalty rather than an expectation.
readings.introduction: Two valid blocks can extend the same parent, and nodes need a rule that makes them converge on one branch. Proof-of-work chains follow the branch with the most cumulative work; when a heavier branch appears, the node reorganizes, and blocks it had accepted stop being canonical. Anything an indexer derived from those blocks must be undone, and anything irreversible should have waited for finality.
readings.nuance: latest can reorg, and safe reflects the consensus client's current view of justified checkpoints. A finalized block can only be reverted if at least a third of all stake is slashed.
readings.objective: Implement a heaviest-chain fork-choice rule, compute a reorganization's undo and apply path, apply confirmation depth, and use Ethereum's safe and finalized tags.
readings.question: After the Merge, which block tag should an indexer wait for before releasing an irreversible withdrawal?
readings.reviewAnswer: finalized: reverting it would slash stake

sections.body: Forks happen without any attacker: two miners find blocks at nearly the same moment, or a proposer's block arrives late. Each node keeps every valid block in a tree keyed by hash, and a fork-choice rule picks one leaf as the head. Longest chain is the informal name, but the rule that resists manipulation is most cumulative work, using the Work value from the proof-of-work lesson, so a branch of fewer, harder blocks beats a branch of more, easier ones. Ties keep the block seen first. The events-finality lesson in the next unit shows an indexer refusing a block that does not extend its tip; this lesson supplies the step that follows, walking both branches back to their common ancestor.
sections.title: Forks are normal; the rule decides

sections.body: Node.Add rejects a block whose parent is unknown or whose height is not the parent's plus one, computes cumulative work and switches head only on strictly more work. route walks the old and new tips back to their common ancestor and returns the blocks to undo, newest first, and to apply, oldest first. The Indexer keeps a small projection, deposit to including block, that it applies and undoes per block, and computes confirmations as head height minus inclusion height plus one.
sections.title: A node and an indexer that survive a reorg
sections.walkthrough: dep-7 lands in A3 and has two confirmations at head A4, below the policy of three, so it is not credited. B2 brings its branch to work 3, not more than 4, so the head stays. B3 brings it to 5, and the node reorganizes via A1: it undoes A4, A3 and A2 and applies B2 and B3, even though A4 is higher. dep-7 then has no canonical block. X9 is rejected because its parent is unknown; a real node would hold it as an orphan until the parent arrives. When B4 re-includes dep-7, its confirmations restart from one.

sections.body: Waiting for k confirmations means waiting until the including block and k-1 blocks after it are all canonical. Under proof of work, the chance that an attacker with a minority of hash rate overtakes a k-block lead falls exponentially with k; the Bitcoin whitepaper works through the numbers, and six confirmations became the convention. It is still a probability, and the right k depends on what is at stake. Recompute confirmations from the current canonical head on every change instead of storing a counter, because a reorg can remove the including block, as happened to dep-7 after B3, or move the transaction to a different height, as B4 did. Identify transactions by their hash, never by block and position.
sections.title: Confirmation depth is a probability policy

sections.body: Ethereum's proof of stake picks the head with LMD-GHOST and finalizes checkpoints with Casper FFG. When validators holding two thirds of the stake attest to a checkpoint pair, the earlier checkpoint is finalized, and reverting it would require at least one third of all stake to be slashed. Normally that takes about two epochs, 64 slots of 12 seconds, a little under 13 minutes. The JSON-RPC tags expose this: latest is the head and can reorg; safe is the block the consensus client expects not to reorg under normal conditions, which clients derive from the latest justified checkpoint; finalized is the latest finalized block. Release irreversible effects such as withdrawals from finalized, and use safe or latest only for views that tolerate rollback.
sections.title: After the Merge: credit from the finalized tag
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs in the reader's own native environment against their own node; it is not executed by the app. ethclient turns the negative rpc.BlockNumber constants into the finalized and safe tags (FinalizedBlockNumber is -3 and SafeBlockNumber is -4 in go-ethereum v1.17.10), so no heights are guessed. store.Finalize is a placeholder for your projection. A stored hash that differs from the finalized hash at the same height means the indexer followed another chain or a misbehaving provider, which calls for an alert, not an automatic rollback.

sections.body: For every block the projection applied, keep enough to reverse it, keyed by block hash: the rows it inserted, or the previous values of rows it updated, like the account journal from the ledger lesson. Undo newest first, then apply the new branch oldest first, in one database transaction together with the checkpoint, so a crash cannot leave a half-reorganized state. Bound the depth you support: below finalized no reorg should happen, and a deeper one is an incident. Finality can also stall when too few validators participate, which has happened on mainnet; then finalized lags far behind latest, and the right response is to wait and alert, not to fall back to latest. Test with scripted block trees like the program's: a one-block replacement, a deep reorg, a heavier but shorter branch, an unknown parent, a re-included transaction and a crash between undo and apply.
sections.title: What an indexer undoes, and how to test it

readings.takeaway: Choose the head by cumulative work, walk to the common ancestor to undo and apply atomically, recompute confirmations from the current head, and release irreversible effects only at finalized.
readings.title: Fork choice and reorgs: follow the heaviest chain and undo what the old branch indexed

cautions: A capped transaction can wait indefinitely while the base fee keeps rising.
Blob gas has a separate fee market that this policy does not bound.
designGuide.cost: A small fee module with table tests and one reviewed ceiling per chain; the price is occasional delayed inclusion during fee spikes.
strengths: Exact integer arithmetic that agrees with go-ethereum's EffectiveGasTip.
A policy ceiling bounds spend even when an oracle or node misbehaves.

readings.hint: One of the two caps starts to bind when the base fee is high.
readings.introduction: Since the London upgrade an Ethereum transaction no longer names one gas price. It carries two caps chosen by the sender, while the protocol sets a per-block base fee that is burned. The price actually paid is decided only when a block includes the transaction, so the code that builds it has to reason about the worst case. This lesson computes those numbers exactly and puts a ceiling in front of the signer that no fee oracle can raise.
readings.nuance: The base fee is burned and the tip is whatever room the cap leaves: with a 62 gwei cap and a 61.5 gwei base fee, only 0.5 gwei of the 2 gwei tip reaches the producer.
readings.objective: Derive maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas with big.Int, predict the effective gas price for any base fee and enforce a fee ceiling before signing.
readings.question: What price per unit of gas does an included EIP-1559 transaction actually pay?
readings.reviewAnswer: min(maxFeePerGas, baseFee + maxPriorityFeePerGas)

sections.body: A type-2 transaction, types.DynamicFeeTx in go-ethereum, carries GasTipCap (maxPriorityFeePerGas, the most the sender offers the block producer) and GasFeeCap (maxFeePerGas, the most it will pay per unit of gas in total). The block header carries BaseFee. A block can include the transaction only if maxFeePerGas is at least that base fee, and the price per gas is then min(maxFeePerGas, baseFee + maxPriorityFeePerGas). The base-fee part is burned; only the remainder reaches the producer. The base fee follows demand: geth's CalcBaseFee changes it by parentBaseFee * (gasUsed - target) / target / 8, so a completely full block raises it by 12.5 percent and an empty one lowers it by the same fraction. Every value here is an integer number of wei that can exceed 64 bits, which is why go-ethereum uses *big.Int throughout and why float64 has no place in the calculation; the exact-units lesson shows that failure for token amounts.
sections.title: Two caps from the sender, one price from the protocol

sections.body: The program takes an observed base fee of 30 gwei and a 2 gwei tip and derives a fee cap of twice the base fee plus the tip, the same headroom go-ethereum's bind/v2 transactor uses when no cap is given. It runs the policy check a signing service would own, builds an unsigned DynamicFeeTx for local chain 1337, and replays the inclusion formula at three possible base fees, cross-checking each result against go-ethereum's own Transaction.EffectiveGasTip.
sections.title: Compute the caps, check the policy, then build
sections.walkthrough: gwei multiplies by params.GWei (1e9) inside big.Int, and formatGwei divides with QuoRem so 61.5 gwei prints exactly. checkPolicy rejects a tip above the cap, a fee cap above 100 gwei and a worst case (gas limit * fee cap) above 0.003 ether: the oracle spike to a 120 gwei base fee yields a 242 gwei cap and is refused, and so is a 200000-gas call even at the normal cap. At base 30 the sender pays 32 gwei and the producer keeps 2. At 61.5 the cap binds, so the producer gets only 0.5. At 63 geth returns ErrGasFeeCapTooLow (fee cap less than base fee) and the transaction simply waits. tx.Cost() is gas * GasFeeCap + value, the balance a node demands up front, not the amount finally charged.

sections.body: In production the base fee comes from the latest header and the tip from the node's suggestion or from eth_feeHistory percentiles. Both are hints from an external dependency, so they are inputs to the policy rather than values the signer trusts. FeeHistory returns one more base fee than the number of blocks requested: the last entry is the node's projection for the next block, a better starting point than the latest header when blocks are full.
sections.title: Take inputs from the node, but let the policy decide
sections.walkthrough: This fragment talks to a real node, so run it in your own native environment against an endpoint whose chain ID you have verified; it is not executed here. HeaderByNumber(ctx, nil) asks for the latest header, and BaseFee is nil before London, which deserves an explicit error instead of a nil-pointer panic. SuggestGasTipCap maps to eth_maxPriorityFeePerGas; the 50th-percentile rewards in hist.Reward are an alternative tip source. hist.BaseFee has blockCount+1 entries, the last one for the next block. Whatever the source, checkPolicy has the last word.

sections.body: Treat the fee ceiling as configuration with an owner, reviewed like any spending limit, and alert when the guard trips instead of raising it automatically. A transaction with 2x headroom can still wait if the base fee keeps climbing; that is the safe failure, because the alternative is paying whatever the market demands. When you do speed up a pending transaction, the replacement rules from the nonces lesson apply: geth's default pool accepts a same-nonce replacement only if both the fee cap and the tip rise by at least 10 percent, so bump both and pass the new values through the same policy. Reconcile budgets from the receipt, EffectiveGasPrice * GasUsed, not from the caps; unused gas and unused headroom are never charged. The gas limit is a separate guard: estimating it is a simulation against current state, and the worst-case fee multiplies it. Blob transactions add an independent fee market, maxFeePerBlobGas, that this policy does not bound.
sections.title: Ceilings, replacements and what is finally charged

sections.body: The fee path needs no node to test. Table-test effectivePrice at base fees below, at and above the point where the cap binds, and assert agreement with EffectiveGasTip in each case so a library upgrade that changes the rules is noticed. Test the guard with a tip above the cap, a zero cap, a cap exactly at the limit (allowed) and one wei above it (refused), and a gas limit that pushes the worst case over the total ceiling. Add a regression test that oracle values are copied rather than aliased: big.Int methods mutate their receiver, so a helper that writes into a *big.Int taken from a header can silently change the next transaction's fees. types.NewTx copies its TxData, which protects the built transaction, but not the policy inputs you keep. In review, check that nothing between the policy check and the signer can change the fields.
sections.title: Test the guard at its edges

readings.takeaway: Compute EIP-1559 fees in wei with big.Int: the price paid is min(maxFee, baseFee + tip), and a policy-owned ceiling on maxFee and on gasLimit * maxFee must reject a transaction before it is signed.
readings.title: EIP-1559 fees: compute the effective gas price exactly and refuse to sign above a ceiling

maxFeePerGas; the producer keeps the whole cap
