readings.hint: Ask what the transaction hash is computed from.
readings.introduction: eth_sendRawTransaction takes one opaque byte string. Everything that matters about a transfer, including its chain, nonce, fees, destination, the signer and its future on-chain hash, is fixed when those bytes are produced, before any node sees them. Producing, checking and storing the bytes offline turns a network call with an unknown outcome into a lookup you can repeat.
readings.nuance: Transaction.Hash is keccak256 of the signed EIP-2718 envelope, so it is fixed before broadcast and lets the service look up a receipt after a timeout instead of signing again with a new nonce.
readings.objective: Sign a typed transaction with a test key, round-trip its raw bytes, recover the sender and use the precomputed hash to make retries safe.
readings.question: A service signs a transaction and its eth_sendRawTransaction call times out. When could it first have known the hash to look up?
readings.reviewAnswer: As soon as it is signed: keccak256 of the raw bytes
readings.reviewPrompt: When is a tx hash known?

sections.body: go-ethereum distinguishes three artifacts. The signing hash, returned by Signer.Hash, is keccak256 over the type byte and the RLP list of fields without a signature; that is what the private key signs. The raw transaction, returned by MarshalBinary, is the EIP-2718 envelope: one type byte (0x02 for EIP-1559) followed by the RLP list that now includes V, R and S. The transaction hash, Transaction.Hash, is keccak256 of exactly those raw bytes. Because the hash is a pure function of the signed bytes, it is known the moment signing finishes, before broadcast, and it does not depend on which node accepts it. The signing-boundaries lesson built an unsigned intent; here it goes through the whole offline lifecycle.
sections.title: One transaction, two hashes and a byte string

sections.body: The example derives a throwaway key from 32 bytes of 0x01, a well-known test key that must never hold funds, and signs an EIP-1559 transfer for local chain 1337. It then plays the receiving side: decode the raw bytes into a fresh Transaction, recover the sender and compare hashes. Two final checks show what stays stable across signing and what changes.
sections.code:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"math/big"

	"github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/common"
	"github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/core/types"
	"github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/crypto"
)

func main() {
	// TEST KEY ONLY: 32 bytes of 0x01. Never fund it or reuse it outside a local chain.
	key, err := crypto.ToECDSA(bytes.Repeat([]byte{1}, 32))
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	from := crypto.PubkeyToAddress(key.PublicKey)
	signer := types.LatestSignerForChainID(big.NewInt(1337))

	to := common.HexToAddress("0x00000000000000000000000000000000000000aa")
	intent := &types.DynamicFeeTx{
		ChainID:   big.NewInt(1337),
		Nonce:     7,
		GasTipCap: big.NewInt(2_000_000_000),
		GasFeeCap: big.NewInt(62_000_000_000),
		Gas:       21_000,
		To:        &to,
		Value:     big.NewInt(1_000_000_000_000_000),
	}
	signed, err := types.SignTx(types.NewTx(intent), signer, key)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	raw, err := signed.MarshalBinary() // the bytes eth_sendRawTransaction carries
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Printf("sender %s\n", from.Hex())
	fmt.Printf("raw: %d bytes, first byte 0x%02x (type %d)\n", len(raw), raw[0], signed.Type())
	fmt.Println("tx hash  ", signed.Hash().Hex())
	fmt.Println("sign hash", signer.Hash(signed).Hex())
	fmt.Println("hash == keccak256(raw):", signed.Hash() == crypto.Keccak256Hash(raw))

	// The receiving side: decode untrusted bytes, then recover who signed them.
	var decoded types.Transaction
	if err := decoded.UnmarshalBinary(raw); err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	got, err := types.Sender(signer, &decoded)
	fmt.Println("recovered sender matches:", got == from, err)
	fmt.Println("decoded hash matches:", decoded.Hash() == signed.Hash())

	_, err = types.Sender(types.LatestSignerForChainID(big.NewInt(1)), &decoded)
	fmt.Println("verify as chain 1:", err)

	again, _ := types.SignTx(types.NewTx(intent), signer, key)
	fmt.Println("re-signed same fields, same hash:", again.Hash() == signed.Hash())

	bump := *intent // shallow copy is enough: we replace the big.Int pointers
	bump.GasTipCap = big.NewInt(2_200_000_000)
	bump.GasFeeCap = big.NewInt(68_200_000_000)
	replacement, _ := types.SignTx(types.NewTx(&bump), signer, key)
	fmt.Println("replacement: same nonce", replacement.Nonce() == signed.Nonce(),
		"new hash", replacement.Hash() != signed.Hash())
}
sections.title: Sign with a fixed test key and round-trip the bytes
sections.walkthrough: LatestSignerForChainID(1337) returns the newest signer in this release, the Prague signer, which accepts every typed transaction and binds signatures to chain 1337. SignTx computes signer.Hash, signs it with crypto.Sign and attaches V, R and S. MarshalBinary yields 119 bytes starting with 0x02, and keccak256 of those bytes equals Hash(). UnmarshalBinary rebuilds the transaction from untrusted bytes, and types.Sender recovers the address; the same bytes checked with a chain-1 signer fail with ErrInvalidChainId. Re-signing identical fields reproduces the hash because go-ethereum signs with deterministic RFC 6979 nonces. Raising both fee caps by 10 percent for the same nonce produces a new hash.

sections.body: The precomputed hash is what makes an unknown send outcome manageable. Store the intent, nonce, raw bytes and hash durably before the first network call, then treat sending as an attempt to publish those exact bytes. After a timeout, ask for a receipt by hash before deciding anything. If none exists yet, resending the stored bytes cannot create a second transfer, because the nonce allows at most one transaction from that account at that position to be included.
sections.title: Persist the bytes and the hash before you send
sections.walkthrough: This fragment needs a node and a database, so it runs in your own native environment; store is a placeholder for your persistence layer. SendTransaction is MarshalBinary plus eth_sendRawTransaction, so the bytes on the wire are the stored ones. The receipt lookup uses the precomputed hash whether or not the send returned an error, and ethclient reports ethereum.NotFound while no receipt exists. On a resend, geth answers already known for a transaction it holds and nonce too low once that nonce is used; the second means some transaction took the slot, so look up the receipt by hash to learn whether it was yours.

sections.body: Three retry strategies look alike and behave very differently. Resending the stored raw bytes is idempotent: same hash, same nonce. Re-signing the same fields is safe only because the result occupies the same nonce. With go-ethereum's deterministic signer it even reproduces the hash, but a remote signer, HSM or KMS that uses random ECDSA nonces returns a different valid signature and therefore a different hash for the same intent, so the record must accept several hashes per nonce. Building a transaction with a fresh nonce is a second payment and belongs to a new business intent, never to a retry; the nonces lesson covers who owns that decision. A fee-bumped replacement deliberately produces a new hash for the same nonce. Whichever version is included wins and the others become permanently invalid, so reconcile by account and nonce as well as by hash.
sections.title: Resend, re-sign or replace: three different retries

sections.body: Services that receive raw transactions from elsewhere, such as a relayer, a co-signer or an approval queue, should decode and check them instead of forwarding bytes blindly. After UnmarshalBinary, compare Type, ChainId, To, Value, Data, Nonce, Gas and both fee caps with the approved intent, recover the sender with a signer for the configured chain and compare it with the expected account. Two details from go-ethereum 1.17 matter in review. Sender rejects a chain mismatch, but SignTx stamps the signer's chain ID onto a typed transaction whose ChainID is zero instead of failing, so the signer, not the intent, picks the chain unless your policy checks ChainID first. And LatestSignerForChainID follows the newest fork of each release, so pin the module version and rerun these round-trip tests on every upgrade.
sections.title: Decode untrusted bytes like a verifier

readings.takeaway: Sign offline, persist the raw bytes and their hash before broadcast, and retry by resending those exact bytes; a fresh nonce is a second payment, not a retry.
readings.title: Raw transactions offline: sign, encode, decode and recover the sender before anything is broadcast
wrongAnswers: Only after a node accepts it into its pool
Only after a block includes the transaction

cautions: Log position fields come from the provider and are not consensus-checked.
Reversal works only while credits are internal; irreversible effects need finality.
designGuide.cost: A per-chain token allow-list, an idempotency key per delivered log and reversal logic in every projection that consumes events.
strengths: Impostor contracts and look-alike events are rejected before money moves.
Duplicate and removed deliveries keep the projection consistent.

readings.hint: Anyone can deploy a contract that emits the same event signature.
readings.introduction: A receipt is the node's report of what a transaction did: whether execution succeeded, how much gas it used and which events contracts emitted. Deposit detectors, payment processors and indexers turn those events into balances, which makes the decoding rules security rules. Anyone can deploy a contract that emits a log shaped exactly like a token transfer, and a log from a block that is later reorganized away has to be reversed.
readings.nuance: Topic 0 only names the event shape. The emitting address proves which contract spoke, the topic count separates ERC-20 from ERC-721, and a reverted receipt has no effects to credit.
readings.objective: Interpret receipt status and gas, decode an ERC-20 Transfer log with accounts/abi, and reject impostor or removed logs before crediting a balance.
readings.question: Which checks must pass before a log is credited as an ERC-20 deposit?
readings.reviewAnswer: Success status, token address, topic0 and 3 topics

sections.body: Receipt.Status is 1 (types.ReceiptStatusSuccessful) or 0 (types.ReceiptStatusFailed). A failed transaction is still included: the sender paid GasUsed * EffectiveGasPrice, the nonce is consumed, and every state change and log from the execution was discarded, so Logs is empty. A successful status only says execution did not revert; whether your business effect happened depends on which logs were emitted and by which contract. Each Log carries the emitting contract Address, zero to four Topics and an opaque Data section. Its block number, block hash, transaction hash and log index are derived fields filled in by the node; go-ethereum's own comment says they are not secured by consensus, so they are only as trustworthy as the provider that served them.
sections.title: What a receipt proves, and what it does not

sections.body: For a non-anonymous Solidity event, topic 0 is keccak256 of the canonical signature, Transfer(address,address,uint256) for ERC-20. Each indexed parameter takes one further topic as a 32-byte word, and the non-indexed parameters are ABI-encoded into Data. The program builds a successful receipt in memory with three logs (a genuine transfer from the expected token contract, the same bytes from an impostor contract and a four-topic log), adds a reverted receipt, then pushes the genuine log through a reorg.
sections.title: Indexed fields live in topics, the rest in data
sections.walkthrough: abi.JSON parses the event, and Event.ID is the topic-0 hash computed from Event.Sig. decodeTransfer checks the emitting address first, then requires exactly three topics with the right topic 0: an ERC-721 Transfer has the same signature and topic 0 but indexes tokenId as a fourth topic and leaves Data empty. UnpackIntoInterface fills only the non-indexed Value from Data, and abi.ParseTopics fills From and To from topics 1 and 2. The reverted receipt is charged a fee and credits nothing. Credits are keyed by block hash and log index, so the duplicate delivery is a no-op, the Removed copy reverses the credit, and the re-inclusion in block B is credited once under its new key.

sections.body: Unpacking event data never reads topics. ABI.UnpackIntoInterface and Arguments.Unpack skip indexed arguments entirely, so a struct decoded only from Data has zero-value From and To fields and no error. ParseTopics wants the indexed arguments alone and the topics after topic 0, and it sets struct fields by reflection from the camel-cased ABI names; if the struct lacks a field, it panics rather than returning an error, so keep the struct next to the ABI and cover it with a test. Indexed strings, bytes and arrays cannot be decoded at all, because the topic holds keccak256 of the value instead of the value. When the ABI comes from a third party, decode with the ABI you reviewed for that deployed address, not with whatever interface the contract claims; the abi-calls lesson makes the same point for calls.
sections.title: Two decoding traps in accounts/abi

sections.body: Push the cheap filters to the node with an ethereum.FilterQuery: the contract address and topic 0 limit what you download, and a topic-2 filter restricts results to transfers into your own addresses. Then repeat every check in the handler anyway. A provider can be buggy or hostile, a query can be widened later by someone else, and the handler is where the money moves.
sections.title: Filter in the query, verify again in the handler
sections.walkthrough: Run this fragment in your own native environment against a node for the expected chain. Topics is positional: the first inner slice matches topic 0, nil accepts any sender in position 1, and the third restricts topic 2, the recipient, to the watched address. FilterLogs returns []types.Log by value, so the loop passes the address of each element. Keep the range bounded, because providers cap block spans and result counts; the events-finality lesson covers backfill and checkpoints.

sections.body: Logs from FilterLogs reflect the canonical chain at query time. Logs delivered through SubscribeFilterLogs or polling filters can arrive twice: once when the block is imported and again with Removed set to true when a reorganization takes that block off the canonical chain. The handler must reverse exactly what it applied, which is why the example keys credits by the delivered log's block hash and log index rather than by transaction hash: the same transaction is often re-included on the new branch at another position and deserves its own credit. Reversal is only possible while the credit is still internal. Anything irreversible, such as shipping goods or withdrawing to another chain, should wait for the confirmation or finality policy from the events-finality lesson. Test the handler with a reverted receipt, an impostor contract, a four-topic Transfer, truncated Data, a duplicate delivery and a removed log whose credit was never applied.
sections.title: Removed logs and what a credit should wait for

readings.takeaway: Credit a token transfer only from a successful receipt, the expected contract address, the exact topic 0 and topic count, and key the credit so a Removed log reverses precisely what was applied.
readings.title: Receipts and logs: decode ERC-20 transfers from the right contract and reverse them on reorg
wrongAnswers: Topic 0 equals the Transfer event hash; nothing else
The ABI decodes the Data section without an error

cautions: ecrecover cannot verify smart-contract wallets; EIP-1271 needs an RPC call.
A login signature must never double as authorization to move value.
designGuide.cost: A nonce table with a TTL and atomic consume, a strict message parser and a test matrix for V, s, domain, expiry and concurrency.
strengths: Password-free logins verified offline with go-ethereum primitives.
Domain binding and single-use nonces defeat relayed and replayed signatures.

readings.hint: The bytes and the signature are identical to the accepted login; only server state has changed.
readings.introduction: Wallets can sign arbitrary text as well as transactions, and many services use that to log users in without passwords. The cryptography is the easy part. A recovered address only says that some key signed some bytes; whether those bytes were meant for your site, for now and for exactly one login is decided by the message format and by state your server keeps. This lesson verifies both halves with a fixed test key and an in-memory nonce store.
readings.nuance: Recovery is stateless and succeeds again for the same bytes. Only the nonce record, deleted when the first login committed, distinguishes the replay from the original.
readings.objective: Verify an EIP-191 personal signature, normalize its V byte, and accept an EIP-4361 sign-in only for this domain, chain and expiry with an unused server nonce.
readings.question: An attacker resubmits a user's valid Sign-In with Ethereum message and signature a minute after the user logged in. What makes the server reject it?
readings.reviewAnswer: A server-issued nonce consumed once, atomically

sections.body: EIP-191 version 0x45, the personal_sign format, prefixes the message with "\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n" and its decimal byte length, then hashes with keccak256; go-ethereum exposes exactly this as accounts.TextHash. The 0x19 prefix keeps the signed bytes from ever parsing as a valid transaction, so a site cannot get a wallet to sign a transfer by calling it a message. The signature is 65 bytes: R, S and a recovery byte V. crypto.Sign returns V as 0 or 1, while wallets and geth's own eth_sign return 27 or 28 for historical reasons, and crypto.SigToPub accepts only 0 or 1. The signing-boundaries lesson argued that recovery is not authorization; this lesson adds the rules that turn a recovery into a login.
sections.title: What personal_sign actually signs

sections.body: The program plays both parties. The wallet side builds an EIP-4361 message, hashes it with TextHash, signs it with a fixed test key and shifts V to 27 or 28 as wallets do. The server side parses the fields it relies on, checks them against its own configuration and clock, recovers the signer and consumes the nonce last. Five attempts show which rule stops which attack.
sections.title: Verify a sign-in end to end
sections.walkthrough: recoverPersonal copies the signature before normalizing V, rejects high-s values with ValidateSignatureValues and recovers with SigToPub over TextHash of the exact message text. Swapping V between 27 and 28 is not detected as malformed: it recovers a different, valid-looking address, so only the comparison with the claimed address catches it, and the nonce survives that failure. The genuine login succeeds and deletes the nonce, so the identical replay fails. A message signed for evil.example fails the domain check even though its signature is perfect, and a message presented six minutes later fails its five-minute expiration. The clock is a fixed value so the output is deterministic.

sections.body: A Sign-In with Ethereum message is plain text with a fixed layout: the requesting domain, the account in EIP-55 checksum form, an optional statement for the user, then URI, Version (1), Chain ID, Nonce, Issued At and optional Expiration Time, Not Before, Request ID and Resources lines. Every value the server compares must come from server state, never from the message: the expected domain and URI from configuration, the chain ID from the deployment, the time from the server clock and the nonce from the server's own store. EIP-4361 requires at least eight alphanumeric characters of nonce; crypto/rand.Text returns 26 base32 characters, which fits. The domain check defeats a phishing site that relays a genuine signature: the wallet shows the user which domain is asking, and your server refuses any domain but its own. Parse strictly against the specification's ABNF and reject duplicate fields, because two parsers that disagree about which Nonce line counts are a vulnerability. The example's parser is deliberately small and skips Issued At and Not Before checks that a real verifier performs with a bounded clock skew.
sections.title: The EIP-4361 fields the server must own

sections.body: The in-memory map and mutex model a single process. A real deployment issues nonces from a shared store with a time-to-live and consumes them with one atomic operation, so two concurrent submissions of the same signed message cannot both succeed. Run the stateless checks and signature recovery first, and make the consume the final step that commits the login.
sections.title: Store nonces so a replay loses the race
sections.walkthrough: This fragment needs a PostgreSQL database, so it runs in your own native environment; db is a *sql.DB and sessionID identifies the pre-login browser session. Binding the nonce to that session stops a signed message captured from one session from being redeemed in another. The DELETE with the expiry condition is the atomic test-and-consume: when two requests race, exactly one sees RowsAffected equal to 1. After a successful login, issue a fresh session identifier instead of promoting the pre-login one.

sections.body: ecrecover verifies only externally owned accounts. A smart-contract wallet has no single private key; it validates signatures through EIP-1271 isValidSignature, which needs an eth_call on the chain named in the message, so supporting those wallets adds an RPC-dependent path with the timeouts and trust questions of the rpc-boundaries lesson. KMS and HSM signers can return a high s value; normalize it (s becomes n - s and V flips) before publishing, because EIP-2 makes high-s transactions invalid and many message verifiers, including this one, reject them. Sign-in proves control of an address at login time and nothing more: map it to an account, issue your own session with its own expiry, and require a fresh, purpose-specific signature or EIP-712 typed data for anything that moves value. Test the verifier with a wrong domain, URI or chain, a missing or past expiration, an unchecksummed address, V of 0, 1, 27 and 28, a high-s signature, a duplicate Nonce line and two concurrent submissions.
sections.title: Limits worth stating in a review

readings.takeaway: A valid signature only recovers an address; a login also needs your domain, URI and chain, an unexpired message and a server-issued nonce that is consumed atomically exactly once.
readings.title: Signed messages and Sign-In with Ethereum: recover the right address and refuse replays
wrongAnswers: The signature no longer recovers the same address
Wallets never produce the same signature twice

cautions: Agreement among providers that share one upstream is a single vote.
AtHash helpers send requireCanonical false; use the raw client when it matters.
designGuide.cost: Extra header calls per pinned read, a provider pool with health state and metrics, and a retry policy that must be tuned and reviewed.
strengths: A lagging or forked provider is detected instead of silently trusted.
Fakes behind the ethclient interface make outage drills instant and deterministic.

readings.hint: Think about what names one chain state unambiguously, even across forks.
readings.introduction: Production services rarely trust one JSON-RPC endpoint: providers have outages, rate limits, stale replicas and occasionally wrong data. Adding a second URL does not fix that by itself. Reads must agree on which block they describe, a provider that disagrees must be detected rather than averaged in, and retries must stop before they turn a provider incident into your outage. This lesson models providers in memory behind the same interface ethclient implements.
readings.nuance: A block number can name different blocks on different forks and latest moves between calls; a hash names one block, and a provider that lacks it fails loudly instead of answering from another state.
readings.objective: Pin multi-provider reads to an agreed block hash, quarantine providers that disagree or lag, and fail over with bounded retries and backoff.
readings.question: Two providers answer latest for different blocks. What makes reads across several providers consistent?
readings.reviewAnswer: Pin every read to one agreed block hash

sections.body: Two providers asked for latest at the same moment can answer for different blocks, and a load-balanced endpoint can serve two consecutive calls from two different backends. A balance from one call and an allowance from the next may then describe states that never coexisted. Pick the block first, usually head minus your confirmation depth or the finalized tag, resolve it to a hash, and make every later read refer to that hash. A read by number lets a provider on another fork answer quietly from its own state; a read by hash, as EIP-1898 allows, fails loudly when the provider does not have that block. The rpc-boundaries lesson already verifies the chain ID and bounds each call; pinning is the next layer.
sections.title: Latest is not a coordinate

sections.body: The program defines Reader as the two ethclient methods the service needs, and a compile-time assertion proves that *ethclient.Client satisfies it, so fakes and the real client are interchangeable. Five fake providers cover the cases: three agree on block 100, one serves a forked header, one is still at block 99, and the first healthy one is rate limited. pin computes each header hash locally and requires a strict majority of all configured providers; balance then reads at the pinned hash with bounded per-provider retries.
sections.title: Outvote, then fail over
sections.walkthrough: Header.Hash() is keccak256 over the RLP of the returned fields, so the client computes it rather than trusting a quoted hash. epsilon has no header 100 and returns ethereum.NotFound, which is what ethclient reports for a null block, so it is excluded rather than counted as dissent. delta's header differs and so does its hash; it is quarantined. Three of five agree, a strict majority. alpha answers every balance call with an rpc.HTTPError of status 429; retryable treats 429 and 5xx as transient, waits 100ms and then 200ms, and after the third attempt moves on. beta answers at the pinned hash. Sleep is injected, so the run is instant and the total backoff of 300ms can be asserted instead of waited for.

sections.body: With real endpoints the shape stays the same: dial each provider with an explicit HTTP client, verify its chain ID before it joins the pool, and wrap it with a client-side limiter so your own traffic stays under the provider's quota instead of discovering the quota through 429 responses.
sections.title: Wire real clients behind the same interface
sections.walkthrough: This fragment dials real endpoints, so run it in your own native environment with URLs from configuration and never with credentials in source. rpc.WithHTTPClient supplies an http.Client whose Timeout caps every HTTP exchange, in addition to per-call contexts. A provider reporting another chain ID never joins the pool. rate.NewLimiter(20, 5) allows 20 requests per second with bursts of 5, and Wait returns an error instead of sleeping past the context deadline. rpc.FinalizedBlockNumber selects the finalized tag; pin then confirms that block hash across providers before any read.

sections.body: Agreement is evidence only if the providers are independent: three brands reselling one upstream are one vote, and the strongest single check is a node you operate or a light client that verifies consensus. Pinning by hash has a subtlety in this release: ethclient's BalanceAtHash, CallContractAtHash and the other AtHash helpers send requireCanonical as false, so a node may answer from a block it still stores after a reorg removed it from the canonical chain. When that matters, call the raw rpc.Client with rpc.BlockNumberOrHashWithHash(hash, true); geth then fails with hash is not currently canonical. Retry only reads and only transient classes (429, 5xx, timeouts), with a per-attempt timeout, an attempt cap per provider and an overall deadline, and add random jitter so many workers do not retry in lockstep; the example omits jitter to stay deterministic. go-ethereum's HTTPError carries the status and body but not response headers, so honoring Retry-After needs a custom http.RoundTripper. Never fail over a send by assuming a timeout meant failure; the raw-transactions lesson explains why.
sections.title: Quorum, canonical hashes and retry budgets

sections.body: Because the service depends on an interface, failure modes are cheap to script: a provider one block behind, one on a fork, one returning 429 for a minute, one that hangs until the context expires, one that returns a malformed header, and all of them at once. Assert outcomes rather than just errors: which provider was quarantined, how many attempts ran, the total backoff, and that no read used a block other than the pinned hash. Export the same facts as production metrics: per-provider error rate by class, head lag in blocks, disagreements per hour and retry budget spent. A disagreement is an incident to investigate, not noise to retry away.
sections.title: Test the pool like a distributed system

readings.takeaway: Choose one block, resolve it to a hash that a majority of independent providers agree on, read only at that hash, and retry transient failures within a fixed budget before failing over.
readings.title: Several RPC providers: pin reads to one block hash, outvote a lagging or lying node, retry within bounds
wrongAnswers: Average the values returned by all providers
Retry each call until two providers return equal values

lessons.explanation: A blockchain's first job is evidence, not consensus: if a past record changes, the change must show. Each block stores the hash of its predecessor, so editing one block breaks the link that points at it. That guarantee holds only when every party hashes the same bytes for the same block, and only when the newest hash is kept somewhere the editor cannot rewrite.
lessons.objective: Link blocks with SHA-256 over a canonical byte encoding, verify the chain from genesis and report the first link that breaks.
lessons.title: Hash chains: every block commits to the exact bytes of the block before it

lessons.explanation: A block header cannot carry every transaction, but it can carry one 32-byte Merkle root that commits to all of them. A client that trusts the header can then check that a particular transaction is included from a handful of sibling hashes instead of the whole block. The tree shape and hashing rules are consensus rules, and two classic mistakes let different transaction lists produce the same root.
lessons.objective: Build a domain-separated Merkle tree, generate and verify inclusion proofs, and explain the duplicate-leaf and second-preimage pitfalls.
lessons.title: Merkle proofs: show one transaction is in a block with about log2(n) hashes

lessons.explanation: A hash chain shows that data changed; a signature shows who approved it. Ethereum and Bitcoin use ECDSA over the secp256k1 curve, and Ethereum appends a recovery byte so that a verifier can compute the signer's public key from the signature instead of receiving it. Recovery always produces some key, so the code that matters is the comparison with the address you expected and the checks that reject malleable signatures.
lessons.objective: Sign a Keccak-256 digest with go-ethereum's crypto package, recover and check the signer's address, and enforce the low-s rule on untrusted signatures.
lessons.title: secp256k1 signatures: sign a 32-byte digest, recover the signer and reject high-s twins

lessons.explanation: An Ethereum address is neither a public key nor a name. It is the last 20 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of an uncompressed public key, written as 40 hex digits. Those digits carry no error detection unless their letter case follows EIP-55, so a validator has to decide what it accepts before value moves: the format, the checksum, and whether the zero address can ever be a destination.
lessons.objective: Derive an address from a public key, produce and check EIP-55 checksums, and validate user-supplied addresses, including the zero address.
lessons.title: Ethereum addresses: 20 bytes of Keccak-256, an EIP-55 checksum and strict input validation

lessons.explanation: Every ledger must answer one question before it accepts a payment: has this value already been spent? Bitcoin answers with a set of unspent transaction outputs that each transaction consumes and creates. Ethereum answers with a balance and a nonce per account that each transaction updates. Neither stores a wallet's balance as a primary fact; both derive it from accepted history, and that choice shapes every indexer built on top.
lessons.objective: Implement minimal UTXO and account ledgers in Go, reject double spends in each, and explain what each model makes easy or hard for an indexer.
lessons.title: Account model versus UTXO: two ledgers and two ways to stop a double spend

lessons.explanation: Ethereum hashes and signs bytes, so every value needs exactly one byte form. On the execution layer that form is Recursive Length Prefix (RLP): transactions, headers and receipts are RLP, and typed transactions are a type byte followed by an RLP payload. RLP encodes byte strings and nested lists and nothing else. go-ethereum's decoder is deliberately strict, because accepting a second spelling of a value means accepting a second hash for it.
lessons.objective: Encode and decode Go structs with go-ethereum's rlp package, recognize the canonical-form rules, and bound untrusted input before decoding it.
lessons.title: RLP: Ethereum's canonical encoding, and why its decoder rejects every other spelling

lessons.explanation: A hash chain reveals that history changed, but anyone can rebuild a chain. Proof of work makes rebuilding expensive: a block counts only if its header hashes below a target, and the only known way to find such a header is to try nonces. Bitcoin still works this way; Ethereum left proof of work at the Merge in 2022. The idea to keep is the asymmetry between expensive search and cheap verification.
lessons.objective: Mine a toy block against a big.Int target, verify it with one hash, compute its expected work and retarget from observed block times.
lessons.title: Proof of work: finding a nonce takes thousands of hashes, checking it takes one

lessons.explanation: Two valid blocks can extend the same parent, and nodes need a rule that makes them converge on one branch. Proof-of-work chains follow the branch with the most cumulative work; when a heavier branch appears, the node reorganizes, and blocks it had accepted stop being canonical. Anything an indexer derived from those blocks must be undone, and anything irreversible should have waited for finality.
lessons.objective: Implement a heaviest-chain fork-choice rule, compute a reorganization's undo and apply path, apply confirmation depth, and use Ethereum's safe and finalized tags.
lessons.title: Fork choice and reorgs: follow the heaviest chain and undo what the old branch indexed

units.summary: Hash chains, Merkle proofs, signatures, addresses, account and UTXO ledgers, RLP, proof of work and fork choice.
units.title: Blockchain foundations in Go
units.translationNote: Local models with reviewed Go libraries and fixed test keys. Nothing here creates a wallet, connects to a node or signs a real transaction.

lessons.explanation: Go is used for blockchain nodes and infrastructure, but a backend that reads balances is not the same system as a validator or a signing service. Start with the target network and the operation you must perform. Prefer the protocol’s maintained libraries, inspect their module boundaries and pin a reviewed release. Adding every blockchain SDK increases dependencies without proving correctness.
lessons.objective: Distinguish RPC applications, transaction tooling and consensus/application frameworks.
lessons.title: Go in blockchain: choose packages by the protocol and the job

lessons.explanation: An Ethereum RPC endpoint is an external dependency with latency, availability and trust limits. A successful TCP connection does not prove that the endpoint serves the intended chain or that every call will finish. Use typed clients, time-bounded operations and an expected chain ID configured by the application. Keep node credentials out of logs and never treat RPC data as authenticated business authority by default.
lessons.objective: Use an explicit RPC client, operation deadline and expected chain identity.
lessons.title: Ethereum RPC: verify the chain and bound every operation

lessons.explanation: Token amounts frequently exceed the exact integer range of float64, even when the human-readable value looks small. Converting through a float before math/big permanently loses information. Parse text under an explicit decimal-scale policy, reject unsupported precision and preserve the integer base-unit value. Token metadata is input to validate, not an instruction to allocate unbounded memory.
lessons.objective: Convert validated decimal text to bounded integer base units with an explicit scale.
lessons.title: Token amounts: parse exact base units without float64

lessons.explanation: An ABI describes how to encode a call and decode its result. It does not prove that the target address has the expected code or that a read result will remain true in a future transaction. An eth_call evaluates a call against a selected chain state without committing it. State-changing execution requires a separate signed transaction lifecycle and can fail even after a successful simulation.
lessons.objective: Distinguish ABI packing, read simulation, signed transactions and deployment identity.
lessons.title: Contract ABI: encoding is not permission and eth_call is not a transaction

lessons.explanation: Two Go workers can read the same pending nonce and sign conflicting transactions. A process-local mutex helps only while one process owns the account; it does not coordinate replicas or survive a crash. Give each business intent a stable identity, persist its nonce and signed transaction identity under one ownership protocol, and reconcile unknown send outcomes before allocating new work.
lessons.objective: Coordinate transaction intent and account nonce allocation before retrying a send.
lessons.title: Nonces, fees and unknown outcomes: one durable owner per account

lessons.explanation: A signing key is authority, not an ordinary configuration string. An RPC URL, ABI helper or generic retry function should not automatically receive it. Separate construction and policy validation from key custody, bind transactions to the intended chain, and record what was approved without logging private keys or seed material. Read-only blockchain work does not require a signer at all.
lessons.objective: Validate transaction intent before delegating signing to an explicitly owned key service.
lessons.title: Signing policy: bind the chain and keep key custody separate

lessons.explanation: A WebSocket subscription is a live notification channel, not a durable ledger cursor. A process can disconnect, a provider can drop a slow subscriber and a chain can reorganize recently observed blocks. Store a checkpoint that includes chain identity and block hash, backfill a bounded range after reconnect and make the projection’s rollback or rebuild behavior explicit.
lessons.objective: Persist canonical checkpoints and reconcile removed or missing events before final effects.
lessons.title: Index events through disconnects and reorgs, not just the happy subscription

lessons.explanation: Since the London upgrade an Ethereum transaction no longer names one gas price. It carries two caps chosen by the sender, while the protocol sets a per-block base fee that is burned. The price actually paid is decided only when a block includes the transaction, so the code that builds it has to reason about the worst case. This lesson computes those numbers exactly and puts a ceiling in front of the signer that no fee oracle can raise.
lessons.objective: Derive maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas with big.Int, predict the effective gas price for any base fee and enforce a fee ceiling before signing.
lessons.title: EIP-1559 fees: compute the effective gas price exactly and refuse to sign above a ceiling

lessons.explanation: eth_sendRawTransaction takes one opaque byte string. Everything that matters about a transfer, including its chain, nonce, fees, destination, the signer and its future on-chain hash, is fixed when those bytes are produced, before any node sees them. Producing, checking and storing the bytes offline turns a network call with an unknown outcome into a lookup you can repeat.
lessons.objective: Sign a typed transaction with a test key, round-trip its raw bytes, recover the sender and use the precomputed hash to make retries safe.
lessons.title: Raw transactions offline: sign, encode, decode and recover the sender before anything is broadcast

lessons.explanation: A receipt is the node's report of what a transaction did: whether execution succeeded, how much gas it used and which events contracts emitted. Deposit detectors, payment processors and indexers turn those events into balances, which makes the decoding rules security rules. Anyone can deploy a contract that emits a log shaped exactly like a token transfer, and a log from a block that is later reorganized away has to be reversed.
lessons.objective: Interpret receipt status and gas, decode an ERC-20 Transfer log with accounts/abi, and reject impostor or removed logs before crediting a balance.
lessons.title: Receipts and logs: decode ERC-20 transfers from the right contract and reverse them on reorg

lessons.explanation: Wallets can sign arbitrary text as well as transactions, and many services use that to log users in without passwords. The cryptography is the easy part. A recovered address only says that some key signed some bytes; whether those bytes were meant for your site, for now and for exactly one login is decided by the message format and by state your server keeps. This lesson verifies both halves with a fixed test key and an in-memory nonce store.
lessons.objective: Verify an EIP-191 personal signature, normalize its V byte, and accept an EIP-4361 sign-in only for this domain, chain and expiry with an unused server nonce.
lessons.title: Signed messages and Sign-In with Ethereum: recover the right address and refuse replays

lessons.explanation: Production services rarely trust one JSON-RPC endpoint: providers have outages, rate limits, stale replicas and occasionally wrong data. Adding a second URL does not fix that by itself. Reads must agree on which block they describe, a provider that disagrees must be detected rather than averaged in, and retries must stop before they turn a provider incident into your outage. This lesson models providers in memory behind the same interface ethclient implements.
lessons.objective: Pin multi-provider reads to an agreed block hash, quarantine providers that disagree or lag, and fail over with bounded retries and backoff.
lessons.title: Several RPC providers: pin reads to one block hash, outvote a lagging or lying node, retry within bounds
